authority: Cambridge Principal Examiner Reports for Teachers, 0500, 17 series 2020-2025.
derivation_policy: Examiner-evidenced errors, restated in our words. No examiner-report wording appears in learner-facing output.
how_to_use: Every entry earns one MISCON card on the objective it attaches to (the work order names the slot). A MISCON card is a DISCRIMINATION: it states the error, the correct move, and the test that tells them apart. It does not simply restate the correct technique.

entries.report_theme: restates in own words rather than copying
entries.learners: copy the text’s sentence when the question asks them to explain in their own words
entries.test: if the key words of the answer are the text’s key words, the idea has been located, not explained

entries.report_theme: explains both parts of a two-part idea
entries.learners: explain one half of a phrase that carries two ideas
entries.test: count the ideas in the phrase before answering; a two-mark explanation that covers one of them is half an answer

entries.report_theme: reads implied meaning as well as stated meaning
entries.learners: answer an implicit question with what the text states on the surface
entries.test: if the question asks what a detail suggests, the answer is something the text does not say in words

entries.report_theme: gives only what is asked; extra material can undo a correct answer
entries.learners: add extra material after the point, some of which contradicts or blurs it
entries.test: stop when the point the marks ask for is made; anything added must be another point, not a padding of this one

entries.report_theme: answers from the part of the text the question names
entries.learners: give a correct idea taken from outside the paragraph the question names
entries.test: an idea from elsewhere in the text can be true and still not answer a question that names its paragraph

entries.learners: string together the text’s own sentences and call it a summary
entries.test: a summary in your own words could be written by someone who had closed the book after reading it

entries.report_theme: selects only relevant points; no examples or excess
entries.learners: include examples and incidental detail as if each were a separate point
entries.test: an example answers “like what?”; a point answers the focus. Several examples of one idea are one point

entries.learners: write a list of unconnected points instead of an organised overview
entries.test: an overview groups and links ideas; if the sentences could be shuffled without loss, it is a list

entries.learners: add their own view or comment to the summary
entries.test: every sentence of a summary should be traceable to the text; a sentence that is not is comment

entries.report_theme: range of points; answers the focus of the question
entries.learners: summarise the topic of the text rather than the focus the task sets
entries.test: test each point against the task’s exact words: on the topic is not the same as on the focus

entries.learners: explain a few ideas at length and run out of words for the rest
entries.test: within a word limit, the number of ideas covered rises as the words per idea fall

entries.report_task: P1 Q2(a) word or phrase with the same meaning
entries.report_theme: the exact word or phrase, not extra text
entries.learners: copy the whole sentence, or explain the meaning, when one word or phrase is asked for
entries.test: the answer is a word or phrase you could substitute for the given idea; a sentence cannot be substituted

entries.report_task: P1 Q2(b) own-words meaning of single words
entries.learners: guess a meaning from how a word looks without checking the sentence it is in
entries.test: put your meaning back into the writer’s sentence; if the sentence no longer makes sense, the meaning is wrong

entries.report_task: P1 Q2(b) own-words meaning of single words
entries.report_theme: own words, not the word itself
entries.learners: repeat the word, or a form of it, in the explanation
entries.test: an explanation that contains the word being explained has not explained it

entries.report_task: P1 Q2(c) one example, explain the effect
entries.learners: discuss several examples when the task asks for one
entries.test: one example fully explained answers the task; three touched on do not answer it three times

entries.report_theme: selects precise words and phrases, not long quotations
entries.learners: quote long stretches of text, leaving no single word examined
entries.test: a quotation is short enough when every word in it is one you comment on

entries.report_theme: explains meaning AND effect, not meaning alone
entries.learners: explain what words mean and stop before saying what they do to the reader
entries.test: after the meaning, ask: so what does the reader see, feel or understand because of this word?

entries.learners: name a device and treat the label as the analysis
entries.test: delete the device’s name from the sentence; if nothing about meaning or effect is left, nothing was analysed

entries.learners: leave an image unexplained, or explain it only literally
entries.test: an image is explained when both the literal picture and what it suggests about the subject are given

entries.report_theme: covers both paragraphs, around three choices each
entries.learners: analyse one paragraph and neglect the other
entries.test: count the choices per paragraph before writing; an answer on one of two paragraphs covers half the task

entries.learners: comment on the atmosphere of a whole paragraph without naming the words that create it
entries.test: every comment should point at a specific word or phrase; a comment that could fit any paragraph is general

entries.report_task: P1 Q3 extended response to reading
entries.learners: cover one bullet fully and another thinly or not at all
entries.test: the three bullets are the answer’s structure; plan a roughly equal share of the words for each

entries.report_task: P1 Q3 extended response to reading
entries.report_theme: develops and evaluates ideas, not just repeats them
entries.learners: repeat the text’s ideas without developing or inferring from them
entries.test: a developed point adds a why or a what-follows that the text supports but does not state

entries.report_task: P1 Q3 extended response to reading
entries.report_theme: uses details from the text, not copying
entries.learners: copy the text’s details instead of using them in their own words
entries.test: the details should come from the text; the sentences they sit in should be yours

entries.report_task: P1 Q3 extended response to reading
entries.report_theme: stays tethered to the text; no invention
entries.learners: invent events or feelings the text gives no grounds for
entries.test: every development should be traceable to something in the text; an idea with no root there is invention

entries.report_task: P1 Q3 extended response to reading
entries.learners: write in a register that does not fit the role or the audience
entries.test: ask who is speaking, to whom, and why; the register follows from those three answers

entries.report_theme: evaluates the ideas, not just summarises them
entries.learners: paraphrase and list the texts’ ideas as if that were evaluation
entries.test: an evaluated point says how convincing an idea is and why; a summarised point only says what it is

entries.learners: draw on one text and ignore the other
entries.test: each text should supply ideas, and each should be used to test the other

entries.learners: lift the texts’ sentences instead of using their ideas in their own words
entries.test: the ideas should come from the texts; the sentences should be yours

entries.report_theme: structure and a line of argument
entries.learners: follow the order of the source texts, so the argument comes out disconnected or contradictory
entries.test: plan by your own line of argument first, then place each source idea where the argument needs it

entries.learners: write a letter, speech or article that reads as a general essay
entries.test: read the opening and closing lines alone; they should tell a reader which form this is and who it is for

entries.learners: handle the second bullet in a single sentence at the end
entries.test: the second bullet is half the task; the evaluation should lead into it, not stop short of it

entries.report_theme: descriptive: images and detail, not a plot
entries.learners: let a description turn into a story told as a sequence of events
entries.test: if the paragraphs are ordered by “and then”, it is narrating; a description is ordered by what is noticed

entries.learners: reach for cliché or showy vocabulary in place of observed detail
entries.test: a precise detail could only belong to this scene; a cliché could belong to any

entries.learners: pack in too many events for the length, so the story has no credible shape
entries.test: in about 400 words one central event, developed, carries a story further than several summarised

entries.report_theme: narrative: character and tension, a real ending
entries.learners: stop the story rather than end it
entries.test: an ending resolves or deliberately leaves open the conflict the story set up; a stop just runs out

entries.learners: use an ambitious word in a sense it does not have
entries.test: a less impressive word used precisely is better than an impressive one used wrongly

entries.learners: join two complete sentences with a comma
entries.test: if both sides of the comma could stand alone as sentences, a comma alone cannot join them

entries.learners: let the tense drift between past and present within a narrative
entries.test: choose the tense of the telling once, and check each verb against it
